entries.title: US-Canada tariff dispute weighs on cross-border ties
entries.summary: As Canada's retaliatory tariffs take effect, Canadian and US car industries fear the trade war will hit them hard, while Canadians are cutting back on travel.
entries.content:
September 8, 2026

As Canada's retaliatory tariffs take effect, Canadian and US car industries fear the trade war will hit them hard, while Canadians are cutting back on travel.

A new suspension bridge connecting the United States to Canada recently opened after more than two decades of planning, but only the Canadians showed up to celebrate. 

The Gordie Howe International Bridge spans the Detroit River, connecting Detroit, Michigan with Windsor, Ontario. It is named after a Canadian hockey player who starred for a US team.

"In normal times, that would be a very, very big celebration, a grand event, with leaders of both countries present," Michigan auto industry spokesperson Glenn Stevens Junior told DW.

But these are hardly normal times in US-Canada relations.

'Escalating tariffs will harm workers'

In July, US President Donald Trump announced a 50% tariff on a wide range of goods from Canada. A second Trump announcement days later of the doubling of tariffs on Canadian automobiles and auto parts to 50%triggered even more concern for businesses on both sides of the new bridge.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney countered with tariffs between 15% and 50% on $20 billion (€17.2 billion) worth of goods imported from the US. 

The retaliatory measures took effect at 12.01 Eastern Standard Time (05:01 GMT/UST) on Tuesday September 8. Polls by the Canadian non-profit Angus Reid suggested that the majority of Canadians were in favor of a tougher stance in tariffs.

At the same time, Canadian workers feared for their jobs, the polls found.

Business leaders, too, have warned of the harmful effects of the tariffs on the economies of both countries.

"An escalating cycle of tariffs and retaliation will ultimately harm businesses, workers, and consumers on both sides of the border," the Detroit-based Canada and US Business Association (CUSBA) said in a statement in response to the tit-for-tat tariff hikes. "Each new tariff compounds costs, disrupts production, delays investment, and weakens the competitiveness of US and Canadian businesses." 

Jobs at stake on both sides of the border

Further north, the Financial Accountability Office of Ontario estimated the new tariff regime will cost 119,000 local jobs in 2026.

Many of these are predicted to be in the auto industry, with Ontario's auto manufacturing output estimated to shrink by 8% in 2026 compared with a no-tariff scenario.

This contraction is expected to be felt on the US side too, especially in Michigan, where more than a fifth of all vehicles produced in the US in 2022 were built, including several well-known household brand names.

The economies of Michigan and Ontario are deeply interconnected, the Detroit Regional Chamber stressed in August.

"Engines that are built in Michigan go into trucks that are built in Ontario, engines that are built in Ontario go into trucks that are built into Michigan," said Glenn Stevens Jr, who is also the chamber's Chief Automotive and Innovation Officer.

Figures show that by 2023, Detroit automakers supported 815,000 indirect jobs through supply chains, as well as 147,000 direct workers across the US.

Detroit's chamber has called for a restoration of "normalcy," defined as a focus on the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, (USMCA, or CUSMA in Canada), due for an annual review.

Tariffs, EV attacks and AI blamed for job cuts

Even before the announcement of Trump's tariffs and Canada's counter-tariffs, Detroit's famous car industry had stalled. 

The volume of production for companies was relatively stable as were jobs on and around auto factory lines, Stevens Jr said.

Although this meant there wasn't a significant loss in employment, new job opportunities weren't being created.

Analyzing the number of US car dealership franchise listings for new vehicles is a standard way of tracking auto production.

These listings show vehicle production has generally increased in the past 12 months, but the past 30 days show a significant slowdown.

Data from industry weekly Automotive News has around 33,000 more listed vehicles compared to this time last year, but 70,000 fewer vehicles were listed in the past month.

Beyond the car showrooms, the US auto industry's cautionary approach is apparent.

US auto companies were adjusting business plans even before the latest round of tariff announcements, with business leaders warning of increased US manufacturing costs.

These costs have now been handed down to the consumers, with US shoppers seeing record sales prices of more than $52,000 for new cars in September.

Companies had resisted hiring people or expanding over the past 18 months since tariff talks between Canada and the US had started to intensify, Stevens Jr said, adding to a lack of investment in new designs owing to withdrawn US federal support for electric vehicles. 

Is cross-border friendship fraying?

Apart from the auto industry, the tariffs are impacting other sectors.

Across the US, real estate market media in June described a "cooling relationship between the two countries," affecting property transactions, tourism revenue and the local economy.

"Most Canadians think it's unpatriotic ... to visit the United States," Claude Molineri, CEO of Visit Detroit said of the cooling friendship and downturn in tourism.

Earlier this year, Detroit's official visitor site reported that the city had seen an 11% decrease in Canadian guests compared to 2025.

Meanwhile, several "buy Canadian first" online campaigns have been referring users to local businesses and Canadian ingredients in everyday grocery items in response to the tariff enouncements.

The cities of Detroit and Ontario's Windsor/Essex normally facilitate trade worth more than $100 billion each year, which is almost a third of all annual trade between the US and Canada, according to Downtown Detroit Partnership, a group of business and community leaders.

The cooling ties between the two countries could come at a heavy price.

Edited by: R. Casey, M. Sass

entries.title: Kenya: Crackdown on foreign traders prompts xenophobia fears
entries.summary: Fears of xenophobia are rising in Kenya after President William Ruto ordered a crackdown on foreigners working as hawkers. The government insists however that legally documented foreign traders remain protected.
entries.content:
Kenya

Kenya: Xenophobia fears amid crackdown on foreign traders

September 8, 2026

Fears of xenophobia are rising in Kenya after President William Ruto ordered a crackdown on foreigners working as hawkers. The government insists however that legally documented foreign traders remain protected.

Kenyan authorities are moving in on some foreign nationals working in the country's informal economy after President William Ruto called for small-scale businesses focused on hawking and petty retail to be primarily reserved for Kenyan citizens.

"We have a bill in parliament [requiring] that there are some trading activities that foreigners can't do in Kenya," he explained, adding that foreign nationals should not come to Kenya to compete with citizens in business settings which need little capital.

The government had announced that the enforcement of this law would begin on Monday, September 7 — and appears to have made good on its pledge.

Ruto framed the latest move as a protection measure for Kenya's economy, highlighting that the focus in the country's economic development should shift to foreign investors who bring capital, create jobs and contribute to local production.

"The investor confidence we have built is for investors, not traders and hawkers. From next week, all traders doing those small businesses should close them," Ruto emphasized, highlighting also that there has been a step increase in informal traders from China in the country.

Mixed reactions to a complex situation

Reactions among Kenyans to these developments have been mixed; some welcomed the crackdown, arguing that foreign traders have been taking away job opportunities in a struggling economy.

"We have been suffering for long. Our jobs are taken," said Nairobi resident James Mwaurah, adding that many Kenyans are unemployed, competing with foreign workers who often are willing to work for lower wages.

"We say thanks to the president for what he has done," Mwaurah added.

Others meanwhile have expressed support for the government's initiative to enforce immigration laws and business regulations, but reject the idea of simply sending foreigners home.

"We accept to have foreigners in our country. Legally, we live with them very peacefully," another local resident, Babu Claudius, told DW on the streets of Nairobi.

In his view, Kenya continues to need foreign workers as well as international business, warning that "chasing them away might scare investors."

Many Kenyans — including Claudius — however seem to agree on one thing: Foreign nationals "have to be here legally."

There are some 17.4 million people who work in Kenya's informal sector, according to official numbers published in 2024; eight in ten of those workers engage in registered business dealings.

For many people, hawking or running a small shop in the informal economy — with or without papers — remains one of the few accessible ways to make a living — including foreigners in the country.

Kenya's mood ahead of elections

Political economist Sheila Owigo Olang says that there is little evidence suggesting "that if you were to kick out the traders, that would immediately result in Kenyan nationals having more opportunities."

According to Olang, there may be other motivations at play, as the new policy appears to come at a "convenient" moment ahead of elections.

In her view, "a lot of it is also just populist," describing the current crackdown on foreign traders as a "feel good policy" ahead of the polls; she highlights that the policy could also serve as a message to external players at this moment: "Foreign investors coil back or they freeze or they wait until the election is finished."

Olang argues that since Kenya wants to keep making itself more attractive to serious foreign investment, it should rather concentrate on tackling broader structural problems instead of focusing on smalltime foreign traders.

"We need to work on corruption. We need to work on our Ease of Doing Business Index so that it's easy to invest within Kenya," she told DW.

The East African country meanwhile attracted a record $3.2 billion (€2.75 billion) in foreign direct investment in 2025 — an increase of almost 38% compared the previous year, according to UNCTAD.

Ruto remains keen to expand on this success story.

A wider push for local opportunities

One approach in Ruto's arsenal is the proposed Local Content Bill 2025, which is currently before parliament. The draft law would require foreign companies covered by the legislation to source at least 60% of certain goods and services locally.

Among other things, it would require at least 80% of their workforce to be Kenyan citizens.

But according to Olang, the measure would not address the roots of Kenya's unemployment crisis, in particular among the country's discontent youth:

The World Bank estimates the unemployment rate among Kenyans aged between 15 and 24 to stand at 15.25%, though local and regional organizations like the Federation of Kenya Employers often cite a much higher figure of roughly two-thirds of all young Kenyans being affected by unemployed and underemployment.

Who is actually affected by the policy?

The government has not published a comprehensive list of businesses that will be affected by the crackdown, as it remains unclear how many foreign nationals could be impacted by the move.

Meanwhile, Kenya's Foreign Affairs Principal Secretary Abraham Korir Sing'oei emphasized that foreign nationals who meet all existing legal requirements, including holding the necessary work permits and licences, will remain legally protected to operate their businesses in the country.

He said that Ruto's current initiative was direcly linked to the introduction of the Local Content Bill, and should not be regarded as a push to get rid of foreigners in the country.

Questions remain over the broader legality of the developments: Under the East African Community's Common Market rules, citizens of member states have the right to move and provide services across the region — though they have to comply with national licensing and other legal requirements.

The debate has also resulted in comparisons being drawn to recent developments in South Africa, where widespread frustration over a sluggish economy has led to foreign-owned businesses and migrants repeatedly being targeted by anti-immigration campaigns this year.

Kenya has not experienced anti-migrant violence on the scale seen in South Africa — yet.

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

entries.title: Australia targets big tech with algorithm opt-out bill
entries.summary: The "My Feed, My Way," legislation would require the likes of Facebook, TikTok and Instagram to let users opt out of algorithms or risk heavy fines.
entries.content:
September 8, 2026

The "My Feed, My Way," legislation would require the likes of Facebook, TikTok and Instagram to let users opt out of algorithms or risk heavy fines.

The Australian government announced planned new rules for social media platforms on Tuesday that would give users greater control over their social media algorithms.

Under the "My Feed, My Way" initiative, social media platforms would have to allow users to opt out of content recommended by an algorithm in their feeds.

What is in Australia's social media algorithm bill?

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese unveiled draft legislation that would impose a "duty of care" on major social media platforms, including Facebook, TikTok, and Instagram. 

Users would only see content from accounts they choose to follow.

"It's not about giving government control. It's about giving people control," Albanese said.

The bill is expected to be approved by the Australian Parliament and introduced later this year.

Companies that do not comply could be fined up to AU$100 million ($72 million, €62 million).

Social media bans for children

Anika Wells, Australia's Minister for Communications, said the measure would help ensure children's safety on social media. Australia became the first country to restrict social media access for under-16s in 2025.

Several countries, including Germany, Spain, France, Denmark, and New Zealand, followed Australia's lead and drafted plans to introduce similar age restrictions. 

Some big tech companies have opposed such new regulations. They argue it could encourage young users to move to unregulated online spaces.

Edited by: Rob Turner

entries.title: Renoir Museum robbery: Three paintings missing
entries.summary: Police are on the hunt for thieves who stole three paintings from the Renoir Museum on the French Riviera in an overnight heist. A fourth stolen work was abandoned as they fled.
entries.content:
September 8, 2026

Police are on the hunt for thieves who stole three paintings from the Renoir Museum on the French Riviera in an overnight heist. A fourth stolen work was abandoned as they fled.

Two thieves have stolen three paintings from the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer on the French Riviera after breaking into the building early on Tuesday, the town's mayor said.

The heist follows a series of high-profile art and cultural-property thefts in Europe.

What happened at the Renoir Museum?

The thieves initially took four artworks, valued together at around €9 million ($10.5 million), but abandoned one as they fled.

The thieves broke into the museum shortly before 6 a.m., Mayor Bryan Masson said.

They were detected with the help of the town's video surveillance system. Police gave chase, but the pair escaped.

"During their flight, they abandoned one of the stolen paintings," Masson said.

Authorities did not immediately identify the three works that remained missing.

The museum occupies the former home and studio of French Impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir, who spent the final years of his life in Cagnes-sur-Mer. The property is surrounded by gardens and olive trees.

What's behind recent art thefts?

The EU's law enforcement agency Europol says typically non-violent specialist gangs are increasingly being replaced by more opportunistic groups, sometimes assembled through social media.

Europol said the groups were driven by the low-risk, high-profit potential of museum heists.

High prices for precious metals, gem stones and other easily resold valuables have also made museums attractive targets.

Recent thefts have involved more brazen tactics, including the use of force or threats. The Louvre theft in Paris last year, in which €88 million worth of jewels were stolen, was cited by Europol as an example of the trend.

Editor: Elizabeth Schumacher

entries.title: PISA test reveals alarming drop in reading and math skills worldwide
entries.summary: The influential global study shows a downward trend in students' performances. Germany is faring worse than ever.
entries.content:
EducationGlobal issues

PISA test reveals alarming drop in reading and math skills

September 8, 2026

The influential global study shows a downward trend in students' performances. Germany is faring worse than ever.

The results of the 2025 PISA study, published on September 8, show a dramatic drop in performance in reading and mathematics around the world.

The Program for International Student Assessment, better known as PISA, is a global study that measures how well 15-year-old students can apply their knowledge and skills in reading, mathematics and science to real-life situations. The test is designed to measure problem-solving skills rather than evaluate students on memorized school facts, which means they cannot revise in preparation for it.

First administered in 2000, it is considered the world's most influential measure of educational performance.

In 2025, more than 760,000 students in 91 countries and economies took the test.

The study always includes in its ranking the average of the international group of 38 advanced, high-income countries that are part of the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, the OECD.

Downward trend in students' performances

Between 2015 and 2025, reading skills have seen the most significant decline, decreasing by 28 points in OECD countries, and by 16 points in the other participating countries and economies.

Scores in math have dropped by 22 points across the OECD on average, compared to a decline of 8 points in the rest of the world.

In science, the focus of the 2025 PISA assessment, a seven-point decline was measured in OECD countries, while the performances in other countries and economies remained broadly stable.

Nearly a third of OECD students considered 'low performers'

The latest PISA study reveals that around 29% of 15-year-olds in OECD countries are now estimated to be "low performers" across all three subjects.

What does this mean?

In science, they struggle to interpret simple data or decipher a graph. In reading, they find it hard to find information in simple texts. In mathematics, they might be unable to understand, for example, the relationship between units and price — basic skills needed for grocery shopping.

Drop in global reading scores most concerning

Across the OECD, reading scores fell by 25 score points on average.

The study points out that 20 score points are about equivalent to a year of learning. This implies that most 15-year-old students were performing at the level typically expected of 14-year-olds.

Among the OECD countries, the drops were most extreme in Iceland and Slovenia, with scores going down by more than 50 points.

Reading scores improved in five countries only: Qatar (up 11 points), Brunei Darussalam (18), Cambodia (26), the Philippines (27) and Zambia (50). Even though these education systems are still below the OECD average, they "deserve recognition for achieving measurable gains despite the broader global decline," notes the study.

Not all schools are equal in Germany

In some countries, such as Iceland, Cambodia and Finland, for example, there is very little variation in performance among schools, showing less than 10% overall variation in student achievement.

But in 10 countries, including Germany, differences among schools account for at least 50% of the total variation in performance.

The study notes that these countries' systems presumably have schools reserved for higher-achieving students, leaving disproportionately large numbers of lower-achieving students enrolled in the other institutions.

For the authors of the PISA study presentation, this is a problem that needs to be taken seriously: "Where such academic segmentation compounds with social background, it can amplify inequalities, producing pockets of excellence while failing to ensure consistent learning outcomes across the education system as a whole."

Germany's PISA shocks

The very first PISA study was held in the year 2000. As one of the 31 participating countries, Germany was shocked to discover that its 15-year-olds scored below the international average.

In the last PISA test, held in 2022 and published in 2023, the scores of German students had dropped to a new low.

In the latest study, scores have plunged even deeper.

Between 2022 and 2025, reading scores plummeted by 15 points and math scores by 11 points, while science scores have gone down by seven.

The top six rankings in reading skills are held by Asian countries. Germany barely remains above the OECD average, coming in 24th. The United States comes in 13th position, Poland ranks 14th and Turkey 18th.

In math, Germany is below the OECD average, coming in 26th, just a rank above the United States. All top seven positions are held by Asian countries, followed by Estonia in the 8th spot.

In science, Germany is only two score points above the OECD average, ranking 23rd. Turkey made important progress in this field, now ranking 19th, with an increase of 18 score points since the 2022 study.

Why is educational performance falling globally overall?

The data itself cannot explain the decline in reading skills, but the authors of the study note that while school closures due to COVID-19 may be one factor, there is no direct relationship between how long schools closed during the pandemic and the students' performances in reading.

There was already a downward trend in many countries long before the pandemic struck, the study notes.

These long-term declines in skills "suggest deeper structural issues within education systems, with challenges at the school and system level," according to the study. These challenges include the impact of digital distractions on students and growing disinterest towards reading books.

AI has had an immediate impact on learning. The 2025 PISA study asked students about their use of AI in schoolwork; more than 40% said they used it to draft texts for writing assignments once or twice a week, or even every day. Students who reported using AI chatbots got lower scores in science, on average, than those who didn't use AI.

"Overall, the data suggests weaknesses in how education systems are adapting to social, technological and economic change," states the study's summary. "Looking ahead, the challenge for policymakers is not simply recovering lost ground, but to ensure schools meet the rapidly changing demands of the world. As PISA shows, it is not an easy task."

While waiting for policymakers to react, the study suggests that parents can contribute to children's potential by being supportive and curious about their studies and helping them develop positive attitudes towards school. "Even something as simple as asking children what they learned or did at school, about once a week or more, is associated with an average 26-point increase in science performance, after accounting for socio-economic status."

Edited by: Brenda Haas

entries.title: Elversberg: Bundesliga newcomers from tiny town make waves
entries.summary: A team from a small southwestern German town of just 7,000 inhabitants made history by sealing promotion to become the 59th club to play in the Bundesliga. Elversberg has got off to a memorable start.
entries.content:
September 8, 2026

A team from a small southwestern German town of just 7,000 inhabitants made history by sealing promotion to become the 59th club to play in the Bundesliga. Elversberg has got off to a memorable start.

How are Elversberg doing in the Bundesliga?

So far, remarkably well. The smallest town ever to be represented in the top flight got off to a dream start on the Bundesliga's opening weekend, racing in to a 3-0 lead against 2024 champions Bayer Leverkusen. In the end, they held off a late surge to claim a 3-2 victory.

A trip to Borussia Mönchegladbach on matchday two looked to have brought them back down to earth, with the hosts leading 3-1 with little over 30 minutes to play. But a sensational comeback was crowned by a Maurice Krattenmacher winner in injury time. The win moved Elversberg above champions Bayern Munich as one of only four sides to have won both their opening two matches, but Krattenmacher was trying to keep some perspective.

"We know every opponent is good in the Bundesliga, but Bayern is on another level entirely. We’ll have to play as a team, and then we’ll see how it goes," he said.

Where is Elversberg?

Elversberg is a small town northeast of Saarbrücken in the small state of Saarland, in southwestern Germany.

As part of Spiesen-Elversberg, the town has a population of around 13,000 but Elversberg alone has just 7,000 people living in it. There is no train station and just three bakeries.

What is Elversberg's back story?

The club was formed in 1907, although folded during World War I before reforming in 1918.

In 2013, the club reached the third division alongside RB Leipzig, but they were promptly relegated. After two playoff defeats in 2016 and 2017, the club finally returned to the third division in 2022 and slowly began to gain a greater reputation.

The club's surge coincided with the appointment of Nils-Ole Book in 2017 and head coach Horst Steffen, a former Bundesliga player, a year later.

Book first joined as a scout before becoming sporting director, where he played a key role in recruitment. Steffen secured back-to-back promotions for the club as they reached the second division in 2023 as a newly-promoted side in the third division.

Germany and Newcastle striker Nick Woltemade played a key role in the club's promotion that year before moving on, and Bayern Munich's Paul Wanner enjoyed a successful loan spell at the club a year later.

In just their second season in the second division (2024-25), Elversberg were in the promotion playoff. But a 95th minute winner from Heidenheim broke their hearts, as they missed out on the top flight. Steffen left for Werder Bremen, star player Fisnik Asllani returned to Hoffenheim and five other key players departed. Not only did it look like the chance had gone, but the club looked more likely to battle against relegation the following season.

How did Elversberg reach the Bundesliga?

Aided by continuity at leading levels of the club, Elversberg found a way to turn a desperate situation into a remarkable one. What proved particularly helpful was having the father-son duo of Frank Holzer, chairman of the supervisory board, and Dominik, the president, leading the way and also calling the shots at main sponsor Ursapharm.

The appointment of head coach Vincent Wagner from Hoffenheim's reserve team was understated, but Wagner did not change much from Steffen's approach. Aided by former Bundesliga legend Mike Frantz, the assistant coach, and team manager Selina Wagner, who won a Champions League with Wolfsburg, the unit off the field appeared as united as the one forming on it.

The departure of star striker Younes Ebnoutalib to Frankfurt during the transfer window and sporting director Book to Borussia Dortmund in March didn't derail the club's promotion ambitions. After losing to relegation battlers Fortuna Düsseldorf in the penultimate game of the season, promotion hopes were wobbling once again. But a win on the final day was enough to keep their spot in second thanks to a superior goal difference. The Bundesliga had been reached.

"A friend of mine told me this week: 'If Elversberg get promoted, then it's like flying to the moon.' Well, today we made it to the moon," Wagner said afterwards.

Where do Elversberg play?

At the Waldstadion an der Kaiserlinde, which has a capacity of 10,000 — more than the population of the town. Construction to reach Bundesliga requirements —15,000 capacity — is reportedly not expected to be finished until 2027, though Elversberg have already been granted an exemption to that rule.

Who are the key figures at Elversberg?

The strength of this team appears to be the collective, and the continuity in leadership positions, rather than one or two individuals.

On the field though, Bambase Conte was signed on loan from Hoffenheim and the attacking midfielder was integral to the club's promotion push. Long-standing goalkeeper Nicolas Kristof enjoyed a strong campaign, as did winger Lukas Petkov who pitched in with 13 goals and seven assists. Striker David Mokwa was bought in January for just €1.5 million, but aided the team down the stretch last term before scoring in the club's first two Bundesliga games.

The squad's average age is 25.3, making it one of the younger squads in the second division. Having reportedly made €10 million from transfers and spent just €3 million on new arrivals, it's clear what this team's approach is. But this summer, it will be intriguing to see how the club approaches the transfer market as it looks to build a squad capable of staying in the Bundesliga.

Edited by: Matt Pearson

This article was updated on September 9, 2026 to reflect Elversberg's strong start to the new Bundesliga season.

entries.title: Female footballers offered egg freezing but doubts remain
entries.summary: Spain's football federation are set to join a handful of clubs in paying for female players to freeze their eggs during their careers. While players have pushed for the move, there are welfare concerns too.
entries.content:
Spain

Female footballers offered egg freezing but doubts remain

September 8, 2026

Spain's football federation are set to join a handful of clubs in paying for female players to freeze their eggs during their careers. While players have pushed for the move, there are welfare concerns too.

Balancing motherhood and work is a challenge in any profession. But for footballers, whose peak sporting years coincide with their peak fertility, the choice can feel stark.

"For a woman whose sports career might last, say, 10 years at a high level, she starts thinking that getting pregnant really isn't an option," former Real Sociedad player, Larraitz Lucas, told DW. "When you are competing at a high level, all you are focusing on is the present."

Until the last few years, only about 2% of footballers got pregnant during their careers, with many leaving the sport to pursue motherhood. But with increasing professionalization, organizations are starting to wrestle with the question of how to deal with players who want to have children.

Binding maternity regulations were introduced to the sport only in 2021 and strengthened in 2024. But for those who wish to postpone their pregnancy while playing, the issue of freezing eggs as a fertility treatment has come to the fore.

US club, Racing Louisville, were the first club side to offer to pay for such treatments in 2021, while English club Chelsea have announced this month that egg freezing will be funded for any player that wants it.

But, perhaps more significantly, the Spanish football federation, RFEF, are expected to become the first national federation to announce a similar policy soon after reported lobbying from star player Alexia Putellas and others.

Playing during egg extraction a tough ask

Such options weren't available to Spaniard Lucas in her playing career, which ended more than a decade ago. While she went through egg retrieval, in her case it was so her partner could have an embryo implanted to carry the baby.

"You keep competing as best you can but no matter how much you try to align it with a weekend break from matches it's tough. Really, before, during, and after the egg extraction, well... it wasn't ideal," said Lucas.

Though it depends somewhat on circumstances, egg freezing can take around three weeks. Women inject themselves every day before their eggs are harvested and frozen under sedation. To use the eggs at a later date, they must be thawed and injected with sperm to create embryos.

But, as athlete gynaecologist, Lamia Zafrani, told DW, egg freezing is far from straightforward. "Egg freezing is not an insurance policy that is guaranteed to pay out. It's always better if you freeze your eggs whilst you're young because you've got younger eggs to then use for future IVF.

"But actually there's no guarantee that when you defrost or thaw those eggs, turn them into embryos, that they'll actually be successful and result in a successful live birth. And I think it's these conversations that the athletes need to be made aware of because, at the end of the day, it's all about informed consent."

Egg freezing 'shouldn't be tool to pressure players'

Zafrani added that the number of athletes in her London clinic asking about the procedure has risen sharply in recent times. "It is definitely something that athletes are very much asking for," she said.

"But there's always nuance to all of these conversations. While it's great because the federations are listening to the players, ethically, it always does bring up the question of whether by offering egg freezing and fertility preservation, the underlying message is that you're telling your players 'don't get pregnant whilst you're working for us.' And that can be problematic."

It's a concern that is shared by Alexandra Gómez Bruinewoud. The legal director of global players' union, FIFPRO, was a co-author of the maternity policies adopted by football's global governing body, FIFA. She said FIFPRO have been working on policies for assisted reproduction, including the freezing of eggs, but that ensuring players were educated about their choices was paramount.

"We don't want it [egg freezing] to be used as a tool to pressure players not to become pregnant while they are playing because they are and they should always be fully entitled to decide when and how to become pregnant," Bruinewoud told DW.

There are, she said, several other considerations with regards to fertility and football, including doping concerns.

"When players go through assistive reproduction in general and if they are going to freeze eggs, in some situations they have to take hormones. And these substances can be prohibited in the WADA (World Anti Doping Agency) code.

"So we want to be sure to prevent a player being sanctioned when they are actually only trying to become pregnant or prepare things to be able to become pregnant in the future," said Bruinewoud.

Universal solution difficult to find

She added that with costs, recovery and procedures varying, mandating one blanket global rule would be near impossible, and should be guided by medical practitioners. It is also tough to apply any universal standard to a sport where professionalization and finance varies significantly between countries.

"In my view, the best solution for that is collective negotiation at national level,” Bruinewoud said. "These are very expensive procedures and most of the players worldwide will probably not have access to this because of the cost."

For all three women, the most important factors are choice, education and empowerment to get pregnant at a time that suits them. The hope is that, if managed well, egg freezing provides another option, rather than the default path.

Edited by: Jonathan Harding

entries.title: India news: Hindu group apologizes over Eiffel Tower row
entries.summary: After the Eiffel Tower was closed amid a staff strike over alleged discrimination, Hindu group BAPS issued an apology, but maintained that no one was denied access. DW has more.
entries.content:
India

India news: Hindu group apologizes over Eiffel Tower row

After the Eiffel Tower was closed amid a staff strike over alleged discrimination, Hindu group BAPS issued an apology, but maintained that no one was denied access. DW has more.

Skip next section Manipur singer killed after confronting group drinking outside Delhi home

Manipur singer killed after confronting group drinking outside Delhi home

A group of men has been apprehended for beating Manipuri musician Chongtham Vikram Singh to death outside his apartment in Southeast Delhi, local media reported.

The 54-year-old lived in Kilokari village, where he was allegedly assaulted by a group of delivery workers and local eatery staff after he confronted them for drinking and creating a nuisance outside his residence, police said.

Seven people have been arrested, and a juvenile has been detained in relation to the assault.

Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi slammed local authorities and Home Minister Amit Shah, raising concerns over the safety of people from the northeastern states of India in Delhi.

"A father, killed outside his own home, in his own country's capital. After many such incidents, every Northeast family in Delhi is asking the same question today - are we safe here?" he wrote on X.

Chief Minister of Manipur, N Biren Singh, also offered condolences to his family, urging Delhi Police to take swift action on the matter. He also shared CCTV footage that claimed to show the accused heading downstairs after assaulting Singh.

The incident has raised concerns among New Delhi's Northeast community. The area that comes under the Sunlight Colony police station is known to have a sizeable population from the region, the Telegraph newspaper reported. In 2023, a group of men assaulted a Manipuri family in the area.

Skip next section Iran hails 'civilizational' relationship with India ahead of BRICS summit

Iran hails 'civilizational' relationship with India ahead of BRICS summit

Iran highlighted its "long-standing, historic and civilizational relationship" with India ahead of President Masoud Pezeshkian's visit to New Delhi for the upcoming BRICS summit.

Iranian Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Esmail Baghaei emphasized the importance Tehran places on its ties with New Delhi during a press conference.

He highlighted President Pezeshkian's bilateral talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, to reaffirm Iran's plans to engage diplomatically with India to deepen economic collaboration.

Referring to the upcoming BRICS summit, he added: "We will certainly make use of the opportunity provided by the BRICS Summit to continue our discussions and consultations with India in areas of mutual interest."

The 18th BRICS summit will be held from September 12 to 13 at the Bharat Mandapam convention center in the Indian capital.

Skip next section BAPS apologizes over Eiffel Tower row, denies preventing access

BAPS apologizes over Eiffel Tower row, denies preventing access

A Hindu religious group has apologized after the Eiffel Tower in Paris, France, was closed on Monday after staff went on strike to protest the exclusion of female workers during a visit by the organization.

The Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS), however, reiterated that their tour was pre-coordinated with the tower's team, adding that no person was denied access. BAPS also offered apologies to anyone hurt or inconvenienced.

"We understand the concerns raised and take them very seriously. Given the size of our delegation, the visit was organised in coordination with the Eiffel Tower team at the beginning of normal opening hours to minimise any inconvenience to other visitors," BAPS said in a statement on social media.

"To our knowledge, at no point was anyone denied access to the Eiffel Tower. Nevertheless, we sincerely apologise to anyone who may have been hurt or inconvenienced by this situation," the statement added.

Around 100 men from BAPS were visiting the landmark. The company that operates the Tower, SETE, said that the group had requested a visit as part of which the "interactions with women" would be limited.

SETE accepted that the decision was a mistake: "These conditions should not have been accepted."

On Sunday, BAPS conducted the consecration ceremony of France’s first traditional Hindu temple in Bussy-Saint-Georges, near Paris.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi virtually addressed the inauguration gathering, adding that "India and France’s relations have reached new heights."

entries.title: Germany news: Gas reserves historically low ahead of winter
entries.summary: Gas storage operator association INES has warned that Germany's gas reserves could run out in the event of a cold winter. Meanwhile, fallout from the AfD's state election victory continues. Follow DW for the latest.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Gas reserves historically low ahead of winter

Published September 8, 2026last updated September 8, 2026

Gas storage operator association INES has warned that Germany's gas reserves could run out in the event of a cold winter. Meanwhile, fallout from the AfD's state election victory continues. Follow DW for the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • German lobby group says gas reserves are at historically low levels and could run out in the event of a cold winter

  • The wars in Russia and Iran have significantly lowered profit margins, thus dampening economic incentive to fill reserves

  • Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said he has no plans of stepping down after the AfD hammered his CDU in Saxony-Anhalt's state election on Sunday

  • Several thousand protesters turned out across the country to voice opposition to the far-right party, which nearly half of Germans say should not be allowed to form a state government

Here are the latest headlines from across Germany on Tuesday, September 8: 

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section German pop singer Xavier Naidoo to be tried for incitement

German pop singer Xavier Naidoo to be tried for incitement

Xavier Naidoo, a German pop singer, will face trial for incitement in an incident involving public antisemitic insults directed at a member of the Amadeu Antonio Foundation — which bills itself as an independent NGO dedicated to strengthening democratic civil society and combating neo-Nazism, right-wing extremism, antisemitism, racism and other forms of bigotry and hate in Germany.

On Monday, a state court in the city of Mannheim, where the musician was born, announced that it would allow state prosecutors to take their case against Naidoo to trial.

Prosecutors sought to bring charges against the celebrity in separate cases in 2023 and 2024, which the court previously rejected for lack of evidence. Prosecutors have lodged a complaint with the Higher Regional Court in Karlsruhe to force the lower court to hear their case on further points.

Monday's decision regards one charge brought in 2023. No trial date has been set.

A popular figure in Germany in the 2000s, Naidoo later made headlines for espousing conspiracy theories, railing against Coronavirus safety measures and hurling antisemitic insults.

In 2021, Germany's top court ruled that Naidoo could be referred to as an antisemite for his song texts. 

In 2022, he released a video statement apologizing for the "many mistakes" he had made over the years, including for "troubling statements," saying he regretted having ever made them.

Skip next section Germany´s exports lose momentum

Germany´s exports lose momentum

Germany's exports were down for the first time in months, the German Federal Statistical Office has confirmed.



For the first time since January,German exports fell by 0.8% due to lower demand from Europe and China.

Germany's shipments to China dropped by 9.5%, while exports to the Eurozone declined by 2.8%. Meanwhile, exports to the United States increased by 19%, continuing a slow recovery following President Donald Trump's tariffs.

Industrial production also declined in July, adding to growing concerns aboutfuel supplies in the country.

Skip next section German students post dismal scores in latest PISA academic assessment

German students post dismal scores in latest PISA academic assessment

The Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) released its 2025 PISA study in Paris on Tuesday and the results are shocking. 

According to the study, overall proficiency in reading, math and science has fallen significantly among 15-year-old pupils in 90 countries, with German pupils faring particularly poorly — posting their worst scores ever in the OECD's Program for International Student Assessment, which has tracked the academic performance since 2000.

"We are seeing historically low levels of proficiency," said Samuel Greiff of the Technical University of Munich.

Released every three years, the 2025 assessment documented a major drop in German students' reading proficiency as well as significant dips in math and science skills since 2022.

"We aren't dramatically behind," said Greiff. "But we are not living up to our own standards as an education nation. We are not among the top performers."

Among the factors contributing to Germany's poor scores were the education system's failings regarding early childhood education, teaching staffing, and digitalization.

Social media use was cited as a particular problem, leading Germany's Federal Commissioner for Drug Issues and Addiction Hendrik Streeck to ask, "How much scientific evidence do we need before we do something? Studies show that early, problematic social media consumption measurably impacts scholastic performance."

Roughly one-third of German students also told pollsters they considered school a "waste of time."

Skip next section AfD victory prompts protests, opposition to party cooperation

AfD victory prompts protests, opposition to party cooperation

Alternative for Germany's (AfD) landslide electoral victory in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday has sparked impromptu protests across the country, with several thousand people turning out in various cities.  

The largest of these took place in Berlin, where regional elections will take place on September 20, drawing an estimated 5,000 participants who exclaimed "fascism is not an alternative."

In a survey conducted by the polling outfit YouGov on Monday, September 7, nearly half of respondents spoke out against political parties working with the AfD to form a state government.

Of the 1,862 people aged 18 and over polled by YouGov, 47% opposed cooperation with AfD, whereas 38% looked favorably upon the proposition.

Germany's domestic intelligence agency has classified the AfD's Saxony-Anhalt branch — which won nearly 44% of Sunday's vote but failed to secure a ruling majority — as "confirmed right-wing extremist."

Skip next section Storage association warns Germany's gas reserves are dangerously low

Storage association warns Germany's gas reserves are dangerously low

Germany's gas and hydrogen storage association INES (Initiative for Energy Storage) on Tuesday said the country's gas storage facilities are at historically low levels as summer heat fades and winter approaches. 

In a paper presented in Berlin, INES said reserves were at 53% of capacity as of early September, the lowest they have been at this point in time over the past 15 years. 

The lobby group said levels could be brought up to 77% by November but only if input is dramatically increased.

INES said 77% capacity would be enough to cover consumer and industry needs if winter temperatures remain normal but added, "77% capacity will not be enough in the event of extremely cold temperatures."

With profit margins minimized by the wars in Russia and Iran, traders have little financial incentive to store natural gas according to INES. Storage facility operators are therefore calling on the German government to lower storage fees.

The Federal Ministry of Economy on the other hand, sees no reason for panic, adding that new LNG terminals off the German coast and pipeline deliveries from Norway can easily cover any potential shortages.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Morgen from DW's Bonn newsroom.

After the drama of Sunday's Saxony-Anhalt state elections we'll look at the fallout from the far-right Alternative for Germany's (AfD) drubbing of competitors as the rest of the country looks on in disbelief. Despite expressing "deep shock," Chancellor Friedrich Merz has vowed to stay in office and forge ahead with his reform program.

Among the other issues that we will cover in the wake of that seismic political result, will be the gas and hydrogen storage association INES' warning that gas storage levels are historically low due to lack of profit incentive, as well as this week's budget battles in Berlin, the presentation of this year's PISA study and pop singer Xaiver Naidoo being charged with incitement.

entries.title: Trump threatens to block Canada's Bombardier planes from US market
entries.summary: Trump says Bombardier must build aircraft in the US as Canada imposes tariffs of up to 50% on US imports.
entries.content:
September 8, 2026

Trump says Bombardier must build aircraft in the US as Canada imposes tariffs of up to 50% on US imports.

US President Donald Trump late on Monday threatened to block Canadian aircraft maker Bombardier from selling planes in the United States unless it manufactures them domestically, escalating a trade dispute with Ottawa as Canada's retaliatory tariffs on billions of dollars in US products take effect on Tuesday.

"NO MORE SELLING ⁠BOMBARDIER ⁠IN THE UNITED STATES! Their products aren't good enough!" Trump said in a post on Truth Social.

"If they want our Market, they must build here, and stop treating America like a 'piggybank',” he said.

He did not specify how a ban would be enforced.

What did Bombardier say?

Bombardier responded to the US president's claims saying it supports tens of thousands of US jobs through its operations and a supply chain of about 2,800 American companies across 47 states.

It also spends more than $2.5 billion (€2.15 billion) annually with US suppliers and said its aircraft use American-made engines, avionics and other components.

Canada's retaliatory tariffs on US goods come into effect

Trump's threat came just before Canada's retaliatory tariffs of up to 50% on $20 billion worth of US imports took effect on Tuesday.

The tariffs cover steel and aluminum products, as well as dairy goods such as cheese.

Ottawa's move came weeks after Trump imposed 50% tariffs on a similar value of Canadian products after Prime Minister Mark Carney refused to match US tariffs on China.
